en: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching to King Prasenajit Regarding His Queen Mother’s Demise and His Body Being Covered in Dust,
translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Dharmakṣema.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Queen Mother of King Prasenajit of the Kośala kingdom passed away; she was then one hundred years old, aged and lacking physical vigor, yet she had practiced the wholesome Dharma with diligence.

At that time, King Prasenajit, having completed the funeral rites for his mother, returned at midday with his body covered in dust. He proceeded on foot to the garden where the World-Honored One was staying, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One asked the king, "For what reason has Your Majesty now come to me on foot, with your body covered in dust?
At that time, King Prasenajit wept uncontrollably; wiping away his tears, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Empress Dowager has passed away, World-Honored One!
The Empress Dowager has entered impermanence, Tathāgata!

She was of an age approaching one hundred years and lacked the vigor of youth; she had long cultivated wholesome dharmas and cherished you with deep affection. Day and night she served you with filial piety, never failing her resolve; yet though life might have been ransomed, she has now lost her body and her longevity.”
If my life can be ransomed by means of elephants, horses, or chariots, I shall provide them all for the ransom;
if my life can be ransomed by means of a multitude of people, I shall likewise provide them for the ransom;
do not let my mother’s life come to an end.
If life can be ransomed by means of gold and silver, one should likewise provide them as ransom;
if life can be ransomed by means of precious jewels, one should likewise provide them as ransom;
if life can be ransomed by means of both gold, silver, and precious jewels, one should likewise provide gold, silver, and precious jewels to ransom life.
If one's life can be saved by ransoming it with a male slave, one should likewise ransom it with a male slave;
if one's life can be saved by ransoming it with a female slave, one should likewise ransom it with a female slave;
if one's life can be saved by ransoming it with both male and female slaves, one should likewise ransom it with both male and female slaves.
If one's life can be saved by redeeming it with a village, one should likewise redeem one's life with a village;
if one's life can be saved by redeeming it with a city, one should likewise redeem one's life with a city;
if one's life can be saved by redeeming it with both a village and a city, one should likewise redeem one's life with both a city and a village.
If one's life can be saved by offering a single province, one should likewise offer a single province to save one's life;
if one's life can be saved by offering the land and its people, one should likewise offer the land and its people to save one's life;
if one's life can be saved by offering a portion of the people, one should likewise offer a portion of the people to save one's life.
"Do not let my mother's life come to an end.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit, saying:
"It is so, Great King!"

"As Your Majesty has said, if my mother's life can be saved by ransoming it with a white elephant, then let us ransom her life with the elephant. If my mother's life can be saved by ransoming it with a chariot drawn by horses, with people, precious gems, gold and silver, slaves, villages, cities, or the inhabitants of a province, then let us ransom her life with the inhabitants of that province; do not let my mother’s life pass away."

"Therefore, Great King, you should contemplate the perception of impermanence; you should cultivate the perception of impermanence extensively; you should cultivate the perception of death extensively.
At that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"All people return to death; there is none who does not die.
According to the deeds one performs, whether calamity or merit, one reaps the fruits of good and evil for oneself.
Hell is for those of evil conduct; the virtuous shall surely be born in heaven."
"Clear wisdom can discern; only merit can restrain evil.
Thus it is, Great King!

There are four fears and great terrors that no one can avoid, nor can they be avoided by force or weapons, nor by incantations, medicinal herbs, elephants, horses, chariots, people, treasures, gold and silver, slaves, villages, cities, or the inhabitants of a region—treasures, gold and silver, slaves, villages, cities, or the inhabitants of a region."
What are the four?
Old age is a great terror; the muscles and flesh waste away, and it cannot be avoided by means of weapons or staffs, nor can even the people of an entire region avoid it.
Illness is a great terror; one loses all vigor and strength, and it cannot be avoided by means of weapons or staffs, nor can even the people of an entire region avoid it.
Death is a great terror; it brings the total end of life and cannot be avoided by means of weapons or staffs, even for the people of a single region.
Parting from those one loves is a great terror; it cannot be avoided by means of weapons or staffs, even for the people of a single region.
"Thus it is said, Great King:

there are these four great terrors which cannot be avoided by means of weapons or staffs, nor by incantations, medicinal herbs, elephants, horses, chariots, or people; nor by treasures, gold, silver, slaves, villages, cities, or the inhabitants of a region; nor by treasures, gold, silver, slaves, villages, cities, or the inhabitants of a region."
It is like this, Great King:
when a great cloud arises with thunder and lightning, it disperses in an instant and does not remain for long.
In the same way, Great King!
The human lifespan is extremely short, with a maximum of a hundred years; those who emerge from it are likewise very few.
It is like this, Great King:

suppose there were four great mountains of solid rock without any gaps, and these four mountains were all equal and began to grind against one another at once; trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs could not be avoided even by means of swords or staves.
Thus it is, Great King!
There are four great terrors that arrive and cannot be avoided.
What are these four?
Old age is a great affliction; the flesh and muscles waste away, and it cannot be avoided by means of swords or staves, nor can it be escaped through medicinal herbs or incantations.
Illness is a great affliction; it destroys the will for vigor and health.
Death is a great affliction; the body is extinguished forever.
The separation from those one loves is a great affliction; it cannot be avoided by means of swords or staves, nor can it be avoided through incantations or medicinal herbs.
Great King!
Cultivate the perception of impermanence extensively; disseminate the perception of impermanence widely.

The reason for this is that one has already cultivated the perception of impermanence and should continue to extend the perception of impermanence; thus, one completely severs all craving for sensual pleasures, completely severs all craving for form, completely severs all craving for the formless, completely severs all ignorance, and severs all craving pertaining to this world as well.
It is just as, Great King,
when a pile of grass, a stack of straw, or a stack of firewood is set ablaze by fire, or likewise a great forest, or a terrace, pavilion, or house— it is the same in this case.

If one cultivates the perception of impermanence and extensively disseminates the perception of impermanence, one completely severs craving for sense-desires, completely severs craving for form, completely severs craving for the formless, completely severs ignorance, and completely severs all craving pertaining to this world.
Therefore, Great King, you should govern by means of the True Dharma;
do not govern by means of what is contrary to the Dharma.
Thus it is, Great King!
"One should train in this way.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is the name of this Dharma?"
"How should it be received and upheld?
The World-Honored One replied:
"It is named the *Sutra on the Removal of Sorrow and Affliction*; this Dharma removes sorrow and affliction."
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
The Sūtra on the Removal of Sorrow and Affliction is thus, World-Honored One!”
The Sūtra on the Removal of Sorrow and Affliction.
Why is this so? World-Honored One, having heard this Dharma, all my longing, grief, and anxiety have been completely eliminated; I perceive for myself that my body has become supple and joyful.
At that time, the World-Honored One fully expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to King Prasenajit, exhorting him to rejoice.
Then, King Prasenajit rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed.
At that time, King Prasenajit of the Kośala country, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on King Prasenajit of the Kośala Country Whose Body Was Covered in Dust Upon the Death of His Queen Mother, Spoken by the Buddha.
